questions.q: Which column on sys.dm_exec_requests directly exposes that a session is being blocked?
options: blocking_session_id
wait_time_ms
cpu_time
logical_reads
questions.explain: It's 0 when a request isn't waiting on another session, and the blocker's session ID when it is.

questions.q: What does the wait_resource column tell you about a blocked request?
options: The specific object, page, or key the request is waiting to acquire a lock on
The total CPU time consumed by the request so far
The name of the database the blocking session is connected to
The exact T-SQL statement causing the block
questions.explain: wait_resource identifies precisely what's being contended for, which helps pinpoint the object involved.

questions.q: Why is a recursive query useful for investigating blocking, rather than just looking at one row of sys.dm_exec_requests?
options: Blocking chains can run several sessions deep, where a blocker is itself blocked by yet another session
sys.dm_exec_requests only returns one row per query execution
Recursive queries are required by SQL Server to read any DMV
blocking_session_id is only populated inside a recursive query
questions.explain: Following blocking_session_id back link by link is how you reach the true root of a multi-session chain.

questions.q: In a blocking chain, what characterizes the root session?
options: It holds the lock everyone downstream is waiting on, and typically has blocking_session_id = 0 itself
It always has the highest cpu_time of any session on the instance
It is always the session with the lowest session_id
It is the session that most recently connected to the server
questions.explain: The root isn't waiting on anyone else — it's simply running something (often a long open transaction) that holds locks others need.

questions.q: In a three-session-deep blocking chain, why does killing the middle session usually fail to unblock the session at the front?
options: The middle session's own blocker (the root) is still holding the lock and hasn't been addressed
Killing a session in SQL Server never actually releases its locks
The front session isn't actually related to the middle session at all
Blocking chains cannot be resolved by killing any session
questions.explain: The middle session was itself waiting on the root — removing it doesn't free the lock still held upstream.
